MATH 119
Calculus with Analytic Geometry
Frequency: Fall/Spring Terms
METU Credit & ECTS Credit: (4-2)5 & 7.5
Catalog description: Functions. Limits and Continuity. Tangent lines and derivatives. Chain rule.
Implicit differentiation. Inverse functions. Related rates. Linear approximations. Extreme values. Mean
Value Theorem and its applications. Sketching graphs. Indeterminate forms and L’Hospital’s rules.
Definite integral. Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Substitution. Areas between curves. Formal
definition of the natural logarithm function. Techniques of integration. Improper integrals. Arc length.
Volumes and surface areas of solids of revolution. Parametric plane curves. Polar coordinates. Arc
length in polar coordinates.
Justification for the Course Proposal: This is a fundamental course designed for all science
and engineering students.
Course Objectives: The sequence Math 119-120 is the Standard complete introduction to the
concepts and methods of calculus. It is taken by all engineering students. The emphasis is on
concepts, solving problems, theory, and proofs. All sections are given a uniform midterm and
a final exam. Students will develop their reading, writing and questioning skills in Mathematics.
Course Coordinator: Dr. Kadri İlker Berktav
• Midterm I (October 24, 2026, Saturday at 11:00) 25 pts
• Midterm II (November 28, 2026, Saturday at 11:00) 35 pts
• Final Exam (January 7, 2027, Thursday at 09:30) 40 pts
• Recitation Quizzes: 7 pts (There will be no make-up for missed quizzes)
• Pearson Tasks: 3 pts (to be accessible via ODTUClass/MATH119AllSections)

below.
For more details about exams and grading, see the announcements on the Course Home page.

Text A-A Shopping Paradise
The city council has finally discovered the secret to creating an attractive city: build more
shopping malls, widen the roads, and replace those inconvenient old trees with elegant
concrete benches. Naturally, residents love spending their afternoons surrounded by traffic
fumes and noise, and nothing brings people together quite like standing in a queue at a shopping
centre. The council is particularly proud of its new public square, where visitors can admire a
magnificent five-storey statue of a family holding huge shopping bags. It expects the square to
become a popular meeting place, especially among people who have just finished shopping or
are about to start shopping!
Tone: ___________________
Text B-Out of Sight, Out of Mind
Every day, thousands of disposable cups, takeaway boxes, plastic bags and unwanted
purchases are thrown away in the city. But why worry? There will always be another bin, another
rubbish truck and, presumably, another place to dump whatever we no longer need. If the
landfill fills up, we can simply find a bigger one. If the streets become dirtier, someone can clean
them tomorrow. After all, rubbish has a remarkable ability to disappear from sight the moment
we put the lid on the bin.
Tone: ___________________
Text C-In whose hands?
City authorities and property developers have turned environmental destruction into a profitable
business, and they expect the public to look the other way. They cut down trees to make room
for shopping centres, cover green spaces with concrete, and fill the streets with traffic, all in the
name of progress. Then, with astonishing hypocrisy, they lecture residents about recycling,
saving water and reducing their carbon footprint. How dare they blame ordinary citizens for
environmental damage while their own decisions make pollution worse every day?!
Tone: ___________________
Text D-The Way We Move
Modern urban design can influence people’s physical activity levels and their risk of obesity. In
deplorably car-dependent cities, residents may rely on private vehicles even for short journeys,
while limited walking routes and inaccessible green spaces can discourage daily exercise. The
World Health Organization (2025) identifies poorly designed urban transport systems such as
disconnected bus and train networks and limited opportunities for walking and cycling as
factors that can contribute to physical inactivity and obesity. Urban planners can address these
health outcomes by investing in pedestrian infrastructure and more accessible transit systems.
Tone: ___________________
Identify the tone of each text below. There are two extra options.
Objective Indifferent Subjective Sarcastic Accusatory Pessimistic
-- 1 of 1 --
